en: *Fenbie lü hanzhù jieben shu fahui ji*,
Scroll Three (From "The Differences in the Placement of Names" to the End of "Correctly Assigning the First Section").
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Shi Yunkan of Shouchang Temple on Mount Tiantai.

"Deeply down. The Buddha, as one possessing all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajña*), discerns the capacities of beings and establishes prohibitions accordingly; he employs these measures only because there is no other way.
"Coarse lashes" refers to the five offenses; they are called "coarse" in contrast to the abbreviated teachings.

"Upon hearing [of transgressions], one should inform [the offender] of the offenses categorized in the Five Groups of Precepts (pañca-āpatti-skandha) so that they may cease their errors. Each case may be treated like the 'willow whip' punishment, which is a form of summary instruction.

'Deep cruelty'—'cruelty' means tyranny or oppression. This may be contrasted with the detailed instructions; thus, the teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism are roughly equivalent. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha's teaching] is universally applicable. The meaning is that the World-Honored One established these regulations by observing the capacities of sentient beings."

For twelve years, the assembly was free from transgression; only the abbreviated teachings were expounded. Thereafter, the faculties of the monks and nuns became inferior, and there were many who violated the precepts.

It became necessary to employ the five categories of grave offenses to subdue and restrain them, as in ancient times when people’s hearts were pure and sincere—when one could mark the ground to form a garden gate and use reeds for a whip.
Soon, however, artifice and hypocrisy arose in abundance, leading to the distinction between the "new" and the "old."
Regarding the five types of offenses (*pañca-vidha-daṇḍa*), if one examines their customary definitions, the intention of the Buddha can be discerned.
The "lower" [category] of *śīla* refers to the subsequent section, as it contains specific designations such as *pārājika*.
As shown in the main text below, this indicates the general designation, because both are referred to collectively as "transgressions," "aggregates," "precepts," and so forth.

Below this, there are generally two types of translations: first, the literal (zheng), and second, the interpretive (yi). Now, it is said that there is no direct equivalent for this term. As for the differences between ancient and modern practices:
here, the Three Miao tribes were cruel and fierce, yet Emperor Mu redeemed their punishments; there, Ajātaśatru committed murder, while Bimbisāra cut off his own finger.

These are all cases where the established laws did not follow old customs, resulting in a harmonious integration of both sides. Thus, the secular penal systems of these two lands may be taken as authoritative models.
Translation: Regarding the "first offense," it refers to the *pārājika*. Because no noble ones (*ārya*) have set foot [in this land], its formal regulation has been abolished;

one may only take the category of the act as a basis and translate it according to its meaning, with nothing remaining. This is because, in contrast to the subsequent *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, which are "with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣa*), this is "without remainder.
As for the phrase "the text says," it points to the introduction of the Vinaya. It states in full: "All those who commit evil deeds are like the dead."
A corpse is something that the community cannot tolerate; for this reason, one must maintain the precepts. Furthermore, the Buddha stated that there are two things with which one may not cohabit:

first, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), and second, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* (confession of precepts). This is logically identical to the principle of being severed from the higher assembly.

"Losing the Way" does not mean being alone; it refers to losing the path to the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*). There are two kinds [of such loss]: namely, the *Prātimokṣa* and the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha. "Rebirth" refers to this present body.

Having been born as a *sadyo-vedanīya* (immediately experienced) retribution, he will not remain in this world for long. How could he not fear the suffering of the *niraya* (hell) for nine hundred twenty-one billion sixty thousand years?

[The text] says "ten below. It states that he falls into an undesirable place. The *Sarvāstivāda* (*Sapoduo*) school explains that this is because he fought with Māra and thereby committed an offense.

This precept would then fall into the category of defeat (*parājika*). Regarding the *Shishi Yaolüe Chao*, it does not clarify this within the sections on the clusters of offenses (*pīn-zhù*); rather, it is recorded separately.

Since it is not clarified here, it should indeed be recorded separately. The *Chao* (the *Shishi Yaolüe Chao*) adopts this for the sake of understanding, as the text of the *Shu* (the *Sifenlü Shanfan Buque Xingshi Chao*) is brief.

This refers to the term "lower. The Sangha explains the meaning of the "upper" Sangha: the preceding [part] provides an equal explanation of the initial meaning of the upper [Sangha], while the final [part] provides an equal interpretation of the remaining meaning of the upper [Sangha].
Thus, the Sangha is the person to whom the confession is addressed; the initial and remaining [parts] are the dharmas bestowed before and after.
This is a name established based on its objective referent (*viṣaya*), because the Sangha is able to remove the offense. Therefore, it conforms to the original Vinaya.
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) should first cite the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which states: "Saṃgha" means the Saṃgha; "Pārājika" refers to what remains, as it is to be dealt with subsequently.

This is evident from the lower section of the Vinaya. In our own Vinaya and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, this is simply termed "Saṃghāvaśeṣa" (Monastic Residue); it differs from the *Samantapāsādikā*, which provides an additional initial interpretation.

The following two lines provide a dual explanation of the meaning of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Saṅgha-remnant). "Having a remnant" (*avaśeṣa*) means that [the offense] is not yet severed. Furthermore, in contrast to the first category [of offenses], these are considered "without remnant" (*anavaśeṣa*).

Moreover, regarding the citation from the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, the name is established based on the initial metaphor; it is because they must be rescued early on that they are so designated. The Vinaya states:
"If one commits this offense, one should be granted the *parivāsa* (probation) and so forth. This is because [these offenses] are adjacent to the grave [offenses].

The *Lüelun* (Summary Treatise) provides the basis for the designation "offense" (*āpatti*) by relying on the reception of benefit; it is only because of these remaining factors that the term is established. According to the *Shichao* (Manual of Ten Matters), the ten [rules] above should have the semantic translation "falling" (*duo*) added as four characters.
Only when this is joined with the explanation from the *Shisong-lü* (Ten Recitation Vinaya) below is the meaning of "falling" fully realized. Thus, the textual intent becomes complete.
Regarding those who must apply effort: the *Śāstra* establishes three types of effort.
First is the effort of guarding against transgression; this means that since names and categories are numerous and modes of conduct are subtle, one is easily prone to violation.
Therefore, one must guard against them.

Second, there is the differentiation by way of the completion of the offense. This means that within these offenses, the nature-based (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the prohibitory (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are intermingled.
For instance, among the simple *pāyattika* (falling) offenses, thirty are designated as nature-based evils and sixty are termed prohibitory precepts; thus, they must be clearly distinguished.

The "three descents" refers to remedial measures through effort, intended to prevent those who have committed offenses from acting extensively. "Great Wailing" (*Mahāraurava*) is the fourth of the six hells.
"Scorching Heat" (*Tapana*) refers to the mental anguish and feverish distress experienced at the time of the initial transgression;
as for the term "result," it points to the blazing fires of the hell itself.
Regarding the term "object" (*viṣaya*) in the phrase "the object of the remedy": this name is established based on the object of the counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*).

Therefore, the scriptural citation provided below follows this principle; the designation "blameworthy" (*nindya*) refers to that toward which one confesses and which belongs to the sphere of the remedy, rather than pertaining to the actual characteristics of the offense itself.

It is as follows. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Duṣ- means 'evil' (*pāpa*), and -kṛta means 'to do. Since this now generally encompasses verbal karma, the term 'evil speech' (*duṣ-kṛta*) is added."

The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states: "All remaining offenses, those shared with the Śaikṣas, and the offenses taught in the Vinaya of Vasu, are all subsumed under the fifth category, the Prāyaścittika. This is the name for the Saṃmitīya school.
Because there are no distinct physical or vocal karmas, the mental [offense] is the *kaukṛtya* (remorse); its opposite is [the non-offense]. Furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins say: 'Duṣkṛta...'"

The two karmas of body and speech are used to correspond with "evil action" (*akuśala-karman*). Although they share the same name, their meanings are distinct. Now, when we speak of body and speech, it is not that there is no movement;
this accords with the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*.
Regarding the Dharma of Medicines: The ancients, following the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* (Chapter on Medicines) of the Vinaya, established five kinds of medicine.

Thus the Vinaya states: "A sick bhikṣu requires the five kinds of root medicines; the Buddha declared that their consumption is permitted," and so forth. Now, one may likewise establish five kinds of instructional medicines. The first category concerns expulsion for defeat (*pārājika*).

The second category concerns the legal procedures of the Saṃgha (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). The third and fourth categories concern the confession through three recitations or one recitation before an individual (*pratideśanīya*). The lower category [concerns the *duṣkṛta* offenses].

Regarding the confession before another and the mental recollection: the ancient masters established these five categories of offenses (pañca-vastu) by prescribing these five kinds of medicinal dharmas to treat the diseases of the five types of transgressions.

If it were argued that the five categories were established based on the five medicines of the Vinaya, then for instance, there should likewise be seven medicines corresponding to the seven groups of offenses (sapta-nikāya).

Furthermore, just as the seven *vinayas* are established to terminate the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), one might argue that seven disputes should likewise be established to correspond to the seven remedies.
Since this interpretation is logically untenable, it is said: "Not so."

This is primarily because the Perfected One (Tathāgata), according to the circumstances of those to be transformed, harmonizes with their capacities and accords with the principle; thus, it is appropriate that he taught five [precepts]. The preceding section reconciles and supports the former interpretation.

This means that the Buddha’s establishment of teachings as medicine is not fixed in its application or exclusion; therefore, one should employ the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) to distinguish them.

Regarding the resolution of the difficulties concerning the seven medicines and the seven disputes mentioned previously, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states that the four wheels are: first, dwelling in a virtuous place; second, ... [text continues] ... .
Relying on virtuous persons: first, one arouses right mindfulness; second, one plants roots of goodness. The first wheel subdues the five difficulties:

being solitary in the three miserable realms, being long-lived [in the heavens], being born at the beginning or end of a Buddha’s appearance, having dull faculties regarding afflictions and wisdom, and being deaf, blind, or mute.

The fourth [wheel] involves the phrase "medicine and disease are both unequal," the wording of which is abbreviated. This is as it is said: all teachings universally serve as the means for various capacities.

Question: Regarding "the lower [category]. Generally speaking, that which is called "medicine" has the function of curing disease. In the lower section, one repents according to the Dharma to eliminate transgressions and restore original purity; thus, the meaning of "medicine" is clear.
In the first section, however, one is subject to extinction and banishment (*pravāsanīya*), which does not constitute the merit of curing disease;

thus, the meaning of "medicine" is lost. How can both be equally termed the "five medicines"? As for those who do not attend to monastic affairs, they are not included in the number of monks eligible for *karmavācanā*; they are merely distinguished by their livelihood.
Regarding the matter of properly extinguishing evil, one cannot reach a definitive resolution.

If that inferior person falsely conforms to the monastic dharma and does not reflect upon their transgressions, they are at fault. If the Saṃgha permits them to enter indiscriminately and thus participates in an improper act alongside them, the Saṃgha itself is at fault.

As for the term *pèn*: the *Tōngsúwén* states that to scatter soil is called *pèn*. Now, this refers to what occurs after the imposition of the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment). Furthermore...
There is no cause or condition by which the Sangha could be defiled, for all people know it to be non-faulty. It is pure and serene (*qingmu*).
According to the *Erya*, "serene" (*mu*) means respectful; it also implies harmony and beauty.

Questioning the latter [part]: If one says that the five categories were established because they correspond to the treatment of the five types of offenses according to their respective teachings and remedies, then there is a slight semblance of purpose.
These two sentences constitute a concession (*yongs*).

Now, I shall present the formal objection. I fear that the medicinal teachings provided may not be sufficient. For instance, among the five categories [of offenses], *sthūlātyaya* is not included; if someone commits such an offense, what medicine will be used to treat it?
Furthermore, regarding the first category [the *pārājika*], there is no confession for an unconcealed offense, whereas a concealed one results in expulsion (*pravāsanīya*).

Thus, two medicines would be added to the first category. This logic must apply equally to the minor offenses down to the *duṣkṛta*, which have both intentional and unintentional violations; the first category should likewise be augmented.
Regarding these two medicines, there is an imbalance in their presence or absence and their quantity. Why, then, is it said that the five medicines correspond to the five categories [of offenses]?
As for "repeated explanation" (*chóngjiè*): looking back to what preceded and assisting what came before, it is called "repeated explanation."
Reaching the section below: treating two ailments simultaneously is called "penetration" (tōng); treating a single ailment alone is called "obstruction" (sè).

Although the offense of *laṅ* is said to reside within the assembly (*jù*), since the time of confession involves both [the assembly] and the face-to-face method (*duìshǒu*), it is also included among the five medicines. Regarding the initial double treatment:
concealment leads to expulsion (*bìn*), which is subsumed under the first medicine; disclosure and the opening of confession are subsumed under the second medicine.

The fourth [category] is a *duṣkṛta* offense committed intentionally against another person; this is also the same as a *pratideśanīya* (confession before another). It corresponds to the fourth medicine.

If one commits it by mistake while intending it for oneself, it falls under the fifth medicine. If this is the case regarding the principles of what is universally applicable versus what is restricted, how could there be any further confusion?

As for the seven methods of settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha*), the method of "being present" (*saṃmukhavinaya*) is universally applicable for extinguishing all four types of disputes, whereas the remedy of "mindfulness" (*smṛtivinaya*) is restrictive. As the text below states: "Only an Arhat free from attachment may employ this."

The Dharma. All other inferior, ordinary methods are not to be relied upon. Regarding the "Three Dharmas" and "Five Dharmas," this refers again to the specific conditions of openness and obstruction within the present medicine itself.
For example, in the case of verbal disputes: an inferior grade is extinguished by the manifestation of three dharmas, while a middling grade requires the manifestation of five dharmas.
If even those medicines are such, one may infer that although there are currently five types of medicine and disease, when it comes to administering the medicine as an antidote, they do not [apply].
There is no distinction between universal and restricted [application]. Therefore, the following section demonstrates the characteristics of the universal and the restricted.

For instance, regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture) which are originally confessed before a single person (*pratimukha*), if it concerns the offense of begging for a bowl, one must confess within the *saṃgha*. Thus, the *Dà cǎo* states: "Within the *saṃgha*-forfeiture offenses, there are two categories:

those involving oneself and those involving others. First, 'forfeiture by oneself': for example, if one begs for cotton to make clothing, one need only cut and destroy it oneself; it does not require the presence of another object. Second...
Regarding the distinction between the ordained and the laity: two types of precious precepts must necessarily be relinquished by laypeople;

the remaining twenty-seven are relinquished in relation to the ordained. Regarding the distinction between the general and the specific: the single precept concerning the begging bowl requires one’s original residence and must be performed through such rites as the distribution of bowls within the Saṃgha;

otherwise, it is not accomplished. The remaining twenty-six apply generally to both [ordained and laity], while the persons involved include both the collective Saṃgha and individuals. Each has its own [distinctions].
The underlying principle is that one cannot apply a single standard to all cases.
Regarding the remaining points, he says: as for the practice of the alms-bowl, a single bowl is sufficient to sustain the body and assist the path toward enlightenment.

Seeking food extensively hinders one's practice and invites derision; one should set aside what is excellent and exchange it for what is inferior. If one does not inform others, there is no way for them to know [of one's needs].

The above are all the master’s accomplishments; they represent the meaning of the ancients establishing medicine in response to illness. Therefore, in the *Vinayamātṛkā* (Introduction to the Vinaya), it says:
"As for why there are five kings, it is because of worldly disputes and litigation; these are what the multitude raise up, the constant law of antiquity.
Those who commit offenses know the law, and those who accord with the law achieve accomplishment. The precepts and the Vinaya are also like this. As it is said:
The King’s governance of the True Dharma was slandered. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Views) states: "We have left the household life and abandoned wealth and sensual pleasure;
we harbor no desire for worldly fame or profit. Why does the Tathāgata, on the contrary, bind us with the *vinaya*?

This will even cause the Dharma to perish quickly," as follows. It further says: "It is like a physician in the world who has not mastered the treatment of illness; seeing a person at the very beginning..."
Suppose an abscess is about to form, but before it has reached the stage of inflammation, one were to burst it prematurely. The patient would say, "I originally had no illness;
you have forcibly burst me open, causing me great agony. The śrāvaka disciples are also like this:

if precepts were established first and then slander arose, they would say, "We ourselves were without fault, yet you have forcibly established these precepts for us. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not establish prohibitions beforehand. This is what is being guarded against.
This refers to the offenses committed themselves, as previously stated. Regarding the two aforementioned teachings, the details necessarily depend on the commission of the offense.
If one follows the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the first four offenses have a fixed sequence, while for the others, the order is not fixed. Now, this refers to that which prevents [the offense].
What reliable basis is there for the sequence of the five categories (*pañcāpatti*)? The Vinaya-holders and those who participated in the various councils [hold this view].
It is the work of a Sage. Regarding the compilation: during the Council of Five Hundred, they gathered all matters concerning bhikṣus in one place to form the Bhikṣu-vinaya;
matters concerning bhikṣuṇīs were gathered in another place to form the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya;
and all rules for ordination were gathered in one place to form the Upasampadā-khandhaka and so forth. This was the codification and arrangement.

Furthermore, the following section concludes the preceding [discussion] and serves as a basis for what follows. The "remedies" (*pratipakṣa*) are the four precepts; they are contrasted with sexual misconduct and the other [unwholesome acts] as the "objects to be remedied.
Regarding the term "net" (*jāla*): the Book says, "When a net is on its main cord (*jāla*), it has its order and is not disordered. "Supporting" (*kuāng*) means to assist.

This refers to the net for the practice of the Dharma within the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses. To escape the state of transgression and restore the way of transformative cultivation is what constitutes thoroughness;
therefore, it is established next [to the preceding category]. Regarding "body, speech, and so forth," this gives rise to the intention of the third section;
from here downward, it belongs to the conduct of majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).
The third chapter of the *Shangxia* (Upper and Lower) concludes here. "Flaw" (*xiá*) refers to a defect within jade. The *Book of Rites* states: "The luster does not conceal the flaw.

From this we know that fine jade is compared in virtue to the gentleman, and the *guī* and *zhāng* ritual vessels are praised by the poets. Therefore, the present statement "without flaw" serves as a metaphor for the purity of a bhikṣu.
If one acts in a lowly manner— such as accepting food, clothing, or other requisites from a nun who is not a relative, or accepting food from various groups of practitioners—

one will be censured by the world. If one does not act in a lowly manner, it is because among the hundred rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*), twenty-six precepts honor the Buddha, eight honor the Dharma, and five...

Eleventh: Reverence for the Sangha. Including the miscellaneous regulations on the four modes of deportment, there are fifteen precepts in total. These various practices constitute the essential fifth section.
Regarding the question below:

the meaning is that the first two sections consist of coarse and manifest matters, which are thus easy to maintain and difficult to violate; when contrasted with the following three sections, however—
Furthermore, this is the opposite of that. Why do you say it is superior? "One-sided" (*yī-gài*) is synonymous with "one end" (*yī-duān*).
The *Liji* states: "Now, speech is not merely one-sided. Kang Cheng’s commentary notes: "'One end' means one-sided."
Furthermore, it is as follows: Once there was a venomous dragon that five hundred arhats were unable to subdue.

An *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) told him, "Worthy one, depart far away. The dragon immediately fled. Someone questioned the arhat about this, and he replied, "It was merely a matter of maintaining the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with equal weight.
Regarding the "Vajra": just as a vajra can crush and shatter objects, so too, although this is a minor precept, it can [accomplish the same].
This destroys pure conduct; therefore, one must rely upon it. Regarding the life-preserving float: in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is likened to riding a float that cannot be plundered by a rākṣasa.
(1) Asking for the whole float is a metaphor for committing the four pārājika offenses. (2) Asking for half is a metaphor for committing the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses.

(3) Asking for the length of a hand-span is a metaphor for committing sthūlātyaya offenses. (4) Asking for the length of a finger-span is a metaphor for committing two pāyattika offenses. (5) Asking for the measure of a speck of dust is a metaphor for minor infractions.
This is analogous to the offense of *duṣkṛta*. It is because that [Bodhisattva] protects both the light and heavy precepts equally.
According to the account of the life-preserving float (*uḍupa*), those crossing the sea in the Western Regions carry a bag of bird feathers or the bladder of a large ox;

if their sea vessel encounters shipwreck, they can blow air into it to buoy themselves up and thus achieve salvation. "Lecturing and discussing" refers to the act of reconciling, adjudicating, and evaluating.
In the section on *Vijñaptimātra*, [the author] refutes the ancients who followed their own minds and attempted to provide universal explanations.
Regarding the phrase "How so," [it refers to] how people of the past sought to define and explain the meaning of "aggregation" (*caya*).
The passage beginning with "If... serves as a further refutation, stating that since these two are not compiled together in one place, they should not be subsumed under the category of aggregation.
Now, "below" refers to the ancients who, based on the present *Prātimokṣa*, designated the multitude of offenses subsumed within the explanatory text as a "collection" (*piṇḍa*).
Now it is not so. The preceding text states: "As in the Vinaya, the five types of offenses are categorized by name. This interpretation is comprehensive and truly possesses profound significance.
"Named collection" (*ming-zu*) means that the names of the offenses are gathered in one place. "Only" (*zhi*) means merely; the intent is that the ancients...

Regarding the statement that "a person in the *vinaya* may be described as a 'collection' (*gaṇa*"): for example, if one does not rely on a person who upholds the *vinaya* during the summer retreat, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense;

such a case should have no presiding authority. Regarding the transgression of the rules of decorum (*iriyāpatha*), the *vinaya* states that one should be dealt with according to the law. This principle applies universally across various characteristics;
how could it be restricted solely to what is subsumed under the name "collection"?
This refers to the "descent," which means to analyze, refute, and distinguish the intent of the five categories (*pañca-vastu*) and the six or seven groups (*ṣaḍ-āpatti-skandha*).

Therefore, regarding what the ancient masters called the "descending" [classification], it refers to the meaning of following the two types of karma—body and speech—and extracting the five groups from above.

Those that cannot be subsumed within these five are then returned to their own respective categories; thus, the two groups of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and *durbhāṣita* (evil speech) are established as distinct karmic positions.

Furthermore, by pairing these two with the five [categories], there are thus seven groups. As for "the measure of the noble" (*ārya-pramāṇa*), this refers to that which is not the measure of the words of a noble person;
how could it be relied upon?
Regarding the phrase "if one says," or if it is said that bodily and vocal misdeeds (*duṣkṛta*) and so forth are used to subsume various offenses, and furthermore, that five groups are distinguished:

If one traces the causes of offenses such as *duṣkṛta*, they exist only in a general form within the concise teachings (*saṃkṣipta-śāsana*) and become extensive only through the detailed regulations (*vistaravidhi*). How, then, can one say they are "extracted" [from the Vinaya]?

Furthermore, if they have not yet been promulgated, or if they do not yet exist prior to the establishment of the detailed rules, yet the general path already possesses offenses such as *duṣkṛta* and *dauḥśīlya*, then [this applies to] laypeople.
Regarding the commission of an offense: it should be classified within the category of *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses).

Furthermore, as for the claim that the detailed teachings were established later and that the specific rules for individual monks were formulated subsequently—since the first precept was only enacted during the winter of the fifth year, at that time there was no indication of a *duṣkṛta* offense, because the detailed exposition had not yet been completed—one should not say this either.

To exclude [the offenses] from the five groups would constitute an obstacle to both advancing and retreating. "Yongni" (use for comparison) means to estimate or gauge. The following section is a rebuttal by way of inversion:
if one says that the latter is borrowed to compare with the former, why stop at the two types of *duṣkṛta*? This is because all seven groups are situated after [the first group].

Furthermore, it is also possible to borrow both together to compare with the preceding offenses, as in the statement: "The *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and so forth, are excluded from the five [groups]."
The "aggregation" may also be accepted, as follows.
From the initial interpretation to the final analysis of separation, all are merely speculative assertions, as follows.

As for the five sense objects such as form and so forth, they are not absent from daily life and thus cannot be dismissed; this is illustrated by the fact that although the meanings of ancient times are clear, [the later views] are still mere conjecture.
They are mutually connected. It is not that one cannot apply [the classification] to the recognition of noble persons; it is because they do not constitute the measure of a sage (*ārya*).
Or, it is established as "lower," meaning it is subsumed according to the specific karmic offenses committed.

As stated previously, there are merely the signs of offenses, differing in their gravity—whether seven or five—and these are collectively subsumed. Or, "lower" refers to the *pārājika* and so forth, as mentioned previously.
This refers to grouping offenses according to their names, which applies across all categories (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*). Regarding those who are deluded:

because sentient beings’ delusions regarding the mind are predominant, the Great Sage opened the mind into four [aggregates] and established one for form; these are collectively named the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Furthermore, for those deluded regarding both mind and form, he opened form into ten and separated the mind into eight, combining them into the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). Moreover, for those whose delusion regarding form is predominant, he thus opened [the elements].

Form is divided into ten; mind is divided into two; thus, together they constitute the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Applying this principle by analogy to other cases, all such classifications are established according to the delusions of sentient beings.
The "three stages" refer to the causes and effects of retribution, ranging from light to heavy.

I shall now definitively explain them in their proper order. Regarding the "Report on the Rebirths," it refers to the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, which compares the lifespans of the six heavens with the karmic retributions for the six classes of offenses.
The *Chao* states: "In formally concluding the sentencing of offenses, only six categories of dharma are established."

Furthermore, the following section indicates the sequence. The treatise states: The opponent says, "Virtuous conduct should come first.

Since virtuous dharmas have sublime fruits, and the practitioner desires to obtain these sublime fruits, one must first explain virtuous conduct and subsequently explain the cessation of evil. The internal [proponent] says, "Next..."
Because it is the nature of phenomena (*dharma*), one first removes coarse defilements and subsequently taints wholesome dharmas and so forth.
Regarding the "three poisons": because greed and the others can harm the wisdom-life of the *dharmakāya* and damage all roots of goodness, they are called "poisons."

The five aggregates are fundamentally empty; to falsely conceptualize them as a self or a person is called "inversion. At present, one is unable to observe this at all, instead falsely grasping at sensory objects and committing transgressions.
This is truly because the three poisons and the inversion of self-view serve as its root. Regarding "evil dharmas," following ancient usage, it should be called "evil matters.

Formerly, the terms "abstaining from what is maintained" and "committing what is transgressed" were used solely to clarify matters within the context of the two teachings [the Pratimokṣa and the Bodhisattva precepts]. Now...

The Master does not agree. The subsequent text states: "The five perversions and seven non-virtues are neither the True Dharma; these practices and matters are no different from [the prohibitions against] killing and stealing.

It further states: "Regardless of whether it concerns a matter or a formal rule, if the Sage prohibits its commission, it applies universally to both observance and transgression; therefore, it may be called an evil dharma."

Ignorance (moha) is the failure to distinguish between good and evil. It violates the original vow made at the time of ordination, which was the aspiration to train in all wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma).
Wholesome dharmas refer, for instance, to the *prātimokṣa* and so forth.

Regarding "essence and form" (*tǐzhuàng*): "essence" (*tǐ*) refers to the essential nature (*tǐxìng*), while "form" (*zhuàng*) refers to the manifest characteristics (*xiàngzhuàng*). These will be explained in detail below.

The interpretation of the ancients—namely, masters such as Yúnhuī and Yuàn—unanimously held that the three types of action (*sānyè*) constitute the essence of both observance and transgression. This is what the *Dàcǎo* (Great Commentary) refers to when it states, "other interpretations have been discarded.
Since the text of the *Cǎo* is concise, I shall now expand upon it in full to avoid leaving those who have not yet awakened in ignorance.
The three evils are lust, theft, and killing. The four transgressions are the two evils of false speech and frivolous speech. The three unwholesome roots are greed, anger, and delusion.
By refraining from these through the three types of action, the essence of the precept of restraint and maintenance is perfected as wholesome.

Bending the body down to the point of releasing living beings constitutes the observance of bodily action (*kāyakarma*). Praising [the act] with the latter two lines constitutes the observance of verbal action (*vākkarma*).

As for the mind below, one cultivates wholesome states such as non-greed; this serves as the antidote so that greed and other afflictions do not arise. Furthermore, by cultivating contemplations such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and relinquishing attachment, one establishes pure conduct.

Additionally, one cultivates the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the four kinds of excellent vows; these collectively constitute mental action (*manaskarma*).
"Active observance" (zuòchí) refers to initiating what follows.

Reversing the above "stills observance" (zhǐchí) constitutes an active offense. "Stills observance" (zhǐchí) refers to ceasing what precedes. Reversing the above "active observance" (zuòchí) constitutes a still offense.
This is followed by the text concerning the releasing of living beings and offering praise, and so forth.

These two were once brothers during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. Because they had cultivated their respective paths with partiality, by the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, the younger brother had become a white elephant and the elder brother had become a bhikṣu.
The brother said to the elephant, "Both you and I have committed transgressions."
The elephant immediately responded to these words. Regarding the passage concerning not eating for three days and so forth, according to the Vinaya:
if one arouses the thought [of remorse] without moving body or speech, but merely reproaches oneself and returns to a state of good intention, this is called "non-offense."
The Four Great Vows are: "Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them," and so on, up to "The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; I vow to realize it.
They are both called "great vows" (*mahā-praṇidhāna*): the term "great" (*mahā*) refers to the vast and universal conditions, while "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) means to restrain one's own mind.

The twelve *dhūta* practices consist of two regarding clothing, four regarding food, and six regarding dwelling; these are explained in detail within the *Dhūta-dharma*. In the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, *dhūta* is translated as "shaking off.
Regarding the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to eliminate the perception of anger toward sentient beings;

one cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) to eliminate the perception of affliction toward sentient beings; one cultivates sympathetic joy (*muditā*) to eliminate dissatisfaction; and one cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*) to eliminate attachment and aversion. Generally speaking...

"Immeasurable" (apramāṇa) is a name derived from the mind following its object. This proves that the meaning is not merely "upholding or violating," but rather that, at the very moment of receiving the fundamental essence, one is unable to specifically adorn it.
If one is inferior, such as not practicing the twelve *dhūta* austerities, one may only be said to engage in practices for self-benefit; thus, one loses the cultivation that accords with principle.
If one does not practice the four immeasurable minds, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), then regarding the practice of benefiting others, one lacks the auxiliary factors of the path.

Furthermore, this does not constitute a violation of the precepts. "Poisonous snake" is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*). The *Śāsanāntima-dharma-sūtra* states: "The poisonous snake of the afflictions sleeps within your heart."
Once the sleeping snake has emerged, one may sleep peacefully.
It is as stated in the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*: "It is like a man or woman whose head or clothing is on fire; they must strive to extinguish the flames immediately.
As long as the fire is not extinguished, they cannot find even a moment’s rest. This, then, refers to the burning of the head. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies the wilderness.

Regarding the metaphor of "saving one's head from fire," it is called "the burning of the head. Here, *ran* (然) is a particle used for emphasis. Thus, we know that the sutra’s parable illustrates the urgency regarding the mind, while the treatise’s analogy refers to liberation.

To say that one is only named "ashamed" (*hrī*) when one quickly seeks liberation because afflictions reside in the mind—yet is called "unashamed" (*āhrīkya*) when one fails to diligently apply antidotes—is incorrect;
furthermore, this does not imply the transgression of precepts. The aforementioned extensive textual evidence proves that the ancient interpretation is entirely erroneous.

Regarding "one who can maintain the mind," it should properly be stated as "one who can maintain [both] observance and transgression. As for "taking the mind as the essence," this is because the essential substance (*svabhāva*) of the karma of observance and transgression must rely on the assistance of the power of the mind to be accomplished.
Therefore, in the precepts of the Hīnayāna, when investigating the transgressions of body and speech, one necessarily questions the mind and so forth.

While body and speech belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and serve merely as instruments (*karaṇa*) for karma, they are not yet capable of constituting the karma itself. Nevertheless, although karma arises from the mind, its manifestation necessarily occurs through body and speech.

If one merely gives rise to body and speech without giving rise to the mind, or merely gives rise to the mind without moving body and speech, in neither case is there either upholding or violating [the precepts].

The *Abhidharmasaṃyuktavastu* (Cheng lun) cites the text from the "Chapter on Right Practice" (*Samyakcaryā-varga*) of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, which states: "Body and speech cannot initiate themselves; they do not arise without depending on the mind.
First, one discerns the preceding object; subsequently, the volitional mind (*cetanā*) arises, stirring and impelling body and speech to perform the preceding action, only then completing the karma."

Therefore, that treatise states: "If one kills without a [premeditated] mind, no physical karma (*kāyakarma*) is established; if one speaks falsely without a [premeditated] mind, no verbal karma (*vākkarma*) is established," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "apart from the mind there is no volition": this refers to the *Abhidharmakośa* refuting the Sarvāstivāda school. According to the tenets of that school, when the mind-king (*cittarāja*) arises, there exists something distinct...
That which is thought by the mind arises simultaneously; it possesses its own substantial entity, and thus our thesis is established. The mind-king and mental factors arise sequentially;
apart from the mind, there is no separate "thought" whatsoever.
Regarding "there being no actions of body or speech": this further refutes the calculations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
They claim that the two types of action—body and speech—do not depend upon the mind but arise from external objects. The Buddha’s teaching is not thus; everything arises from the mind.
Regarding the "two kinds": this means that both upholding and violating each have two aspects.
As for the following question: "Generally speaking, that which is upheld applies to all objects, because at the time of receiving the precepts, the mind encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.

After receiving them, among the myriad phenomena that appear in profusion, what could possibly not be upheld? Why, then, do you now clarify this in terms of the two teachings? Answer: This is in reference to the objects [of the precepts].

Although numerous, they do not depart from two teachings, which encompass them all completely. Depending on the object confronted, there is no distinction made between sentient and insentient beings, nor between wholesome, unwholesome, matters, or dharmas.
If it is not an object for which creation or prohibition is prescribed, it is an object for which permission to act or permission to refrain is prescribed.

When the mind arises in relation to an object, merely by conforming to the two teachings one fulfills the two types of observance (*dhāraṇī*), and by violating the two teachings one incurs the two types of transgression.
Thus, it is known that observance and transgression cannot be distinguished on their own; one understands their boundaries only by reference to what is prescribed and what is permitted.

Since these two teachings encompass all objects, their true nature is clarified through the dual framework of prescriptions and permissions. As for the essence of that which is observed, it resides in the object.
This is as explained in detail in the *Huizheng lun* (Treatise on Rectifying Deviations).

Regarding evil—such as the unwholesome acts of sexual misconduct, theft, and so forth—one is enjoined not to commit them. Because the mind accords with the teaching, the practice of "abstaining from what is prohibited" (*zhi-chi*) is accomplished.

There are wholesome factors, such as the robes, alms bowls, and the teachings of the Tripitaka. If one practices in accordance with the teachings, then the performance of upholding and practice is accomplished.
This is merely a brief indication of the general outline; therefore, it is called "the broad summary."

Contrary to the lower [category]. For example, within the prohibitive teachings (*pratiṣedha-śikṣā*), because one acts in violation of the prohibited matters, the "prohibitory observance" (*virati-dhāraṇa*) is inverted to become an "active offense" (*kriyā-āpatti*).

Furthermore, within the prescriptive teachings (*vidhi-śikṣā*), if one is negligent and fails to study the prescribed methods, the "prescriptive observance" (*anusthāna-dhāraṇa*) is inverted to become a "non-active offense" (*avirati-āpatti*).

"Regarding 'making' (kṛta): the term 'making' accords with the gate of listening (*śravaṇa-mukha*); 'not making' resides in superior practice (*adhi-caryā*). Therefore, it is not an offense. Regarding 'having':
as in matters such as sexual misconduct or theft, both the karma and the transgression are grave; thus, they are prohibited. Regarding 'non-existence':

as in matters such as dwellings or robes, since there is no affliction when following the teachings, their making is permitted. This single phrase precisely reveals that in all cases of making or not making, there is no fault."
Furthermore, if one distinguishes between the two teachings, they are differentiated solely within the gate of listening (*śravaṇa*) regarding what is to be practiced and what is to be ceased.

Thus, the text below states: "Regarding these dharmas of the matter, there is both listening to practice and listening to cessation. For example, if one possesses a dwelling or wealth, it is logically necessary to apply the ritual procedure (*vidhi*); therefore, it is 'listening to practice.
If there are obstacles or difficulties, or if the clothing or wealth would lead to transgression, it is not appropriate to apply the ritual procedure; therefore, it is 'listening to cessation.'"
Regarding the "lower" [teaching]: why must both the prohibitive (制) and permissive (聽) teachings be established for those of middle capacity?

It is simply because if one were to employ only the prohibitive teaching to guide sentient beings, those of superior faculties would benefit, while those of middle and lower capacities would be excluded from the path; thus, the teaching would be too restrictive.

Conversely, if one were to employ only the permissive gate, even those of superior faculties would be suppressed and reduced to the level of the middle and lower; thus, the teaching would be too lax. Therefore, both teachings are required.
The ritual accordingly accords with the three capacities [of practitioners]. This principle may be sought in the cases of Subhūti, Garbha, Kāśyapa, and others.

Second, regarding the two teachings, these refer to prohibitions and permissions. Regarding the subsumption of dharmas, this refers to the selection and inclusion of specific matters. Ancient masters, based on the dharmas, restricted this to the categories of active observance (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*) and abstaining from transgression (*vārya-āpatti*).

From the perspective of the dharmas, they did not extend this to the scope of abstaining from observance (*vārya-dhāraṇa*) and active transgression (*kṛta-āpatti*); thus it was termed "delimitation" (*sīmā*). According to the present masters, however:

Both matters (*vastu*) and dharmas (*dharma*) are common to the four types of conduct (*caturvidha-ācāra*), which serve as their respective boundaries. However, with respect to the side of following the teachings and avoiding transgressions, it belongs to *śīla-dhāraṇa* (maintaining through restraint);
acting in accordance with the teachings is *kriyā-dhāraṇa* (maintaining through performance). If one violates these two, both types of offenses are incurred. Regarding the boundary of matters:

examples such as the four grave offenses (*catur-parājika*) constitute matters of maintaining through restraint and committing offenses within the prohibitive teachings (*pratiṣedha-śāsana*). Matters such as improper dwellings or extra robes constitute the permissive teachings (*anujñā-śāsana*).
Abstaining from performing transgressive acts is intended so that one does not fail to accord with the Dharma; hence it is said, "only.

According to the present master, based on the seven non-prohibitions and five heterodox practices (*pañca-kudṛṣṭi*), abstaining constitutes observance (*dhāraṇa*), whereas performing them constitutes a transgression. Thus, the Dharma also applies to these two modes of conduct.

Second, the matters of the teachings (*śāsana*). These include the recitation of the precepts (*prātimokṣa*), formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), and such things as robes and alms bowls according to the Dharma;

these are the matters of performing, maintaining, ceasing, and transgressing within the *pratikṣepa-śikṣā* (prohibitive teachings). Examples include the formal authorization (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), the construction of a dwelling, and the prescribed dimensions;

these are the matters of performing, maintaining, ceasing, and transgressing within the *anujñā-śikṣā* (permissive teachings). Since the matters and the laws herein encompass all aspects equally, they are called "universal" (*sāmānya*). The preceding section refers to the aforementioned "ceasing and maintaining" and "performing."
Regarding the two types of transgressions: why is it that some apply only to specific matters and do not extend to the Dharma?

As for the "Dharma" mentioned below, according to the ancient masters, all such Dharmas refer to the wholesome teachings of the Tripitaka and so forth. One must exert effort in cultivation and study before they can be fully understood.
Therefore, because they accord with the teachings, they are subsumed under "active observance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*); because they oppose the teachings, they are [subsumed under] "cessation" (*virati*).
The category of "cessation through transgression" (zhìfàn shè) does not encompass "cessation through observance" (zhǐchí) or "action through transgression" (zuòfàn).

Regarding "matters" (shì): in cases such as sexual misconduct or theft, which are evil deeds, the focus lies solely on abstaining from them; since one naturally refrains from committing them, these are subsumed under "cessation through observance."
One must certainly maintain [the precepts]; if one violates the teaching, one naturally incurs an offense.

Therefore, the conclusion below states that "active maintenance" (作持) involves both the matter and the dharma, whereas "restraint through non-action" (止持) is restricted to the matter and does not extend to the dharma; this is why they differ.
The five perversions and seven non-prohibitions, as clarified below, are all contrary to the Dharma and must logically be restrained.
How can it be said that the observance of prohibitions (*śīla*) and the commission of offenses apply only to specific matters?

Regarding "matters" (vastu): this refers to what was previously stated—that matters merely involve distancing oneself from faults and encompassing the dharmas through self-restraint. This can only be known through diligent cultivation.
Since one does not yet discern whether a dharma is wholesome or unwholesome, the meaning would be inconsistent [with the principle]. Now, however, it is not so:

it simply ensures that wholesome matters and wholesome dharmas are subsumed under "active observance" (kṛta-śīla) and "restrained non-transgression" (vārita-avadya), while unwholesome matters and unwholesome dharmas are subsumed under "restrained observance" (vārita-śīla) and "active transgression" (kṛta-avadya).

Regarding the classification by level below: this distinguishes the categories according to the stages of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), thereby clarifying the nature and characteristics of the ritual procedures (*karmavastu*) through the two teachings of prohibitions and permissions that do not exceed these limits.
A brief explanation: The reason why we first establish what "should not be learned" (*akṣeya*) now is entirely different from the ancient tradition.

From the very beginning of Master Yunhui’s *Shoushu* (Commentary on the Fundamental Precepts), he has consistently clarified that within the category of "abstaining and maintaining" (*zhi-chi*), one first explains what "should not be learned. This refers to all evil deeds;

because they are not permitted to be learned or practiced even within a clear and conscious mind, they are termed "not to be learned. Because one does not perform them, this constitutes "abstaining and maintaining. Thus, evil is ceased and goodness is established.

This is the sequential order of their meanings. Therefore, the second [category] clarifies that which "can be learned," because all wholesome matters must be learned. Now, the Master’s position is not thus;
he maintains that regarding all matters of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, one must first learn to know them clearly within the mind.

Thus, "that which can be learned" is placed first. Subsequently, when confusion and forgetfulness arise regarding what has been understood, one fails to comprehend it due to those conditions; therefore, "that which cannot be learned" is placed last.

As for the three objects: humans, non-humans, and animals. As for the four subjects: the Three Jewels, humans, and non-humans and animals. Regarding sexual misconduct, if one commits it toward all three objects, the offense is a *pārājika*;

therefore, it is called "universal" (*sāmānya*). Regarding theft, because the offenses incurred toward the four subjects vary in their exclusion, they are divided. This refers to the observance of restraint.
Within the teachings of the Middle Vehicle, the prohibitions govern matters; the mind becomes clear and capable of learning.
Furthermore, when our present teacher treats sexual misconduct and theft as subjects for study, it is essential to understand both of these positions.
Regarding the five deviations: in the Vinaya, Devadatta propounded five deviations in order to subvert the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). These are: begging for food for as long as one lives;
wearing rag-robes; sitting in the open air; not consuming ghee or salt; and fifth, not eating fish or meat for as long as one lives.
Regarding the "seven non-[proper actions]": In the Vinaya, the *karmavācanā* excludes these seven non-proper acts, which constitute *adharma-vinaya*.

They are: 1) *adharma* with a separate assembly; 2) *adharma* with a harmonious assembly; 3) *dharma* with a separate assembly; 4) *dharma-like* with a separate assembly; 5) *dharma-like* with a harmonious assembly;
6) [the seventh is] not ceasing after being rebuked seven times. This differs from the interpretation established in the *Sìshāo*.
"Delusion" (*mí*) refers to fundamental delusion; "inversion" (*dǎo*) refers to erroneous inversion, such as claiming one has not committed an offense when one has.

"Following" (*suí*) refers to following along with objects such as the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), failing to discern them correctly—all these are termed delusive inversion. This includes, for example, perceiving property that has an owner as being ownerless.
However, because the action has not yet been performed, it is termed "cessation" (*zhǐ*).

Regarding the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*): their essential characteristics, such as wearing rag-robes and begging for food, are identical; however, they are conflated by looking toward the limit of "lifelong adherence.

"Forgetting the lower" refers to being deluded regarding the three aforementioned dharmas, mistaking the false for the correct, and having no certainty in one's contemplative mind; yet, with respect to the limit of "not yet having acted," it is still considered correct.

"Holding" is not "inferior. This explains the meaning of the name. Although the textual phrasing differs from the preceding section, the principle is the same. This refers to the prohibitive rules within the "teachings of restraint" (制教) under the category of "abiding in observance" (止持).
When one acts out of delusion or forgetfulness, it constitutes a violation that cannot be excused as a mere lack of learning.
Answer: Regarding the section below, this refers to one who does not study the teachings; such a person is deluded regarding the teachings but not deluded regarding the mind.
According to the conduct that has been impaired, one adds the *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and *ajñāna-sthūlātyaya* (grave offense through ignorance) to the root offenses.
Now, the following section concerns delusion of mind versus non-delusion regarding the teaching. Previously, these matters were clearly and thoroughly explained;

however, it is solely due to the arising of a deluded or forgetful mind that one fails to understand the fundamental and the derivative aspects of the conditions. In such cases, there is no offense, as stated below:
when making the three robes and the single alms bowl, the cloth must be of fine silk, gauze, or thin fabric, and the dimensions must conform to the Buddha’s measurements.

This includes the five primary colors and so forth. Regarding the alms bowl, it must not be made of materials such as gold, silver, lacquer, or wood; nor should it exceed or fall short of the prescribed measurements, nor should it be dyed with vermilion.

This constitutes the "prohibitive instruction" (*niyama-śikṣāpada*) within the category of "maintaining prohibitions" (*vāritasamvara*). When clearly understood in the mind, this becomes a matter of training (*śikṣā*).

As follows: one trains in the single *pācittiya*, the two *pācittiyas*, and the four *pācittiyas* as prescribed by the Noble One. When performing these actions, one must avoid the seven improper ways.

This is the method of composition within the "teachings on prohibitions" (*pratiṣedha-śikṣā*) among the "observances of restraint" (*saṃvara-śīla*). It is clear that this can be learned within the mind.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it would logically have been appropriate to further establish two phrases regarding "that which cannot be learned," based on both phenomena and principles; that these are not explained here is because [they were already covered] previously.

It has already been clarified within the section on the Dharma of Prohibitions (*zhi-zhi*) that [certain matters] are not to be practiced; this can be understood by analogy, and is therefore omitted here.

This is also like the section on the Gates of Observance and Prohibition (*zhizhi-zhimen*) in the *Shuochao*, where, among those things that are to be practiced, two categories are established—observance (*zhizuo*) and prohibition (*zhizhi*)—but subsequently only one category, "not to be practiced," is established, thereby making it clear that both observance and prohibition regarding specific matters may involve what is not to be practiced. The present case is the same.
Regarding the meaning of the question: it is said that, in general, "abstaining and maintaining" (*zhizhi*) has the sense of guarding against and refraining from evil deeds.

Now, if there were "action" within this "abstention," how would it differ from "maintaining through action" (*zuochi*) mentioned below? Furthermore, if one were to clarify "action" here, then "abstention" and "action" would become conflated and confused.
[Question: It is chaotic. How should it be categorized?

[Answer: Although the discussion here concerns the performance of actions, the underlying intent lies in the accomplishment of *śīlavṛtta* (observance of precepts). This is like the training and regulation regarding the possession of robes and alms bowls.

Anticipating that one currently possesses [the robes], this constitutes "active observance" (*kriyā-śīla*). Not violating the rule against lacking robes is called "restraint observance" (*virati-śīla*). Complying with and reverently following the teaching is likewise "active observance.
Thus, within restraint there is active observance, and active observance subsumes restraint; the fundamental principle is clear and distinct. How could this be considered confused?

The answer below states: There are instances where wholesome *samvara* (restraint) arises that belongs equally to both *kriyā* (action) and *dhāraṇa* (maintenance). This meaning is identical to the original [definition] because it serves to establish *saṃvara* (abstinence).

However, the specific intention of "action" is distinct; this is similar to cases such as practicing meditation while abstaining from sexual misconduct. The principle regarding the dual aspects of maintaining and violating the precepts lies herein.

"Double observance and double transgression" refers to the mutual citation of one by way of abbreviation. To speak of "double observance" is to abbreviate "double transgression," as the text below states:
"Violating these two observances constitutes both transgressions. To speak of "single transgression" is to abbreviate "single observance," as the text below states:
"Lacking the virtue of sacred teaching"—these are all instances of single observance.

The function of the mind. "Mind" here refers to the active mind; "function" refers to its efficacy. For example, when one gives rise to a mind of wholesome action, its efficacy encompasses both the observance and the commission of precepts.
When one gives rise to a mind of unwholesome action, its efficacy likewise encompasses both the violation and the commission of precepts.

[The text] omits the characters for "minor offenses" below. For instance, regarding the first precept, guarding it according to the established teachings constitutes "observance through virtuous conduct," which achieves *śīla* (restraint).

If one can contemplate impurity so that revulsion becomes manifest, such that even when coerced by an enemy, there is no defiled pleasure—like one [fleeing] from a snake's mouth or a fire—this constitutes "observance through action," achieved through virtuous conduct.
To transgress these two states of mind is, conversely, to commit both types of violations.
This constitutes an offense. As it is with one precept, so it is with all precepts. "Teaching" refers to the two types of instruction: prohibitions and permissions.
"Practice" refers to the conduct explained by those teachings; it necessarily arises based upon objective conditions such as robes, alms bowls, and dwellings.

Regarding "relying on the lower [teachings]," within the two types of instruction—prohibitory and permissive—the performance of what is prescribed and the abstention from what is forbidden constitute the two aspects of dual observance (*ubhayasamvara*).

Conversely, those who perform what is prescribed and abstain from what is forbidden without such scriptural authority possess only single observance (*ekasamvara*). Therefore, it is said: "Acting in accordance with the teachings.

As for the section beginning with "What is it?", this infers and explains the reason for dual observance. It may be considered similar to the prohibitions against killing and stealing; however, there is only the observance of abstinence (*virati*) that accords with the teachings. Violation...

The instruction regarding the commission of an offense establishes the meaning of both the "single possession" (*ekadhāraṇa*) and "double possession" (*ubhayadhāraṇa*) offenses. How could there be an instructional text that permits the act of "making" while establishing the meaning of "possessing"?
Since the instruction for this robe and bowl is already established as being "made," it therefore possesses both types of possession.

Question: Regarding the lower category, if one says that relying on an object while complying with the teaching constitutes non-offense and is termed "active observance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇa*), then as in the case where sexual misconduct is permitted when one is coerced by an enemy, since one has united with the object yet looks toward the prohibitions of the teaching to restrain the mind, it may be termed "active observance";
however, because one does not experience defiled pleasure, it should be designated as "restraint observance" (*vārita-dhāraṇa*).
Does this, then, also possess both types of observance (*dhāraṇī*)?

it refers to a case where a bhikṣu, having committed sexual intercourse with a celestial maiden, felt doubt. The Buddha said, "This is a pārājika offense. This is what is meant.
Regarding the gravity [of offenses]: namely, killing, sexual misconduct, stealing, and false speech. Why are these not equal? Regarding the dragon pearl:

This refers to the mind’s continuous application and movement toward the objective field; this is termed progression. "One should not raise the objection that striking oneself, slandering oneself, and so forth do not constitute an offense, because the precept still remains intact. This refers to cases where [the act] has not yet...

Regarding the single category of *kṣaṇa* (definitive) offenses, based on their arising as described above, they should properly be placed in the seventh [category].

Even if one intends a human object, should the encounter later occur with a non-human or an animal, the full formal offense (*sāpattika*) is incurred in every case.

Regarding "the object and the mind both shift": this refers to cases where there is no person and yet one suspects there is a person; or where the object differs and the mind shifts, such that both conditions are absent.

This is because the precept against sexual misconduct does not depend on the correspondence between the actual object and the perception; even if these conditions are lacking, one still commits the offense. Otherwise, it would imply that the precept against sexual misconduct does not distinguish between intentional and unintentional acts, treating them equally as grave offenses.

"Feeling the holy one" (*gaṅ sheng zhě*) carries the meaning of attaining the fruits of realization; thus, the *Śū* (Commentary) itself cites the conditions for Tan-ni’s entry into the state of holiness, as will be clarified below.

Regarding "obstructing the path" (*zhàng dào zhě*), it refers to obstructing the four fruits of the śramaṇa. To distinguish between the specific (*kè*) and the general (*màn*): killing and stealing are specific offenses;

violating sexual misconduct is also a formal bond (*jié*) in its general sense, which can be understood accordingly. "Corresponding" (*xiāng dāng*) means, for instance, when a person kills another person, or when property belonging to an owner is treated as having an owner [and thus stolen].

The phrase "the subject perceives it as theft" constitutes the first clause within the classification of perceptions regarding the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*). This demonstrates that when the mental intent is specific and determined, a grave offense is incurred.

Regarding the subsequent four clauses—such as when one doubts whether the victim is a human or a non-human—the offense is not of the fundamental category; rather, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
This indicates that such cases involve a distracted or indeterminate mind, and thus the offense is light.
"Mutually" refers to others and enemies. Although one may overcome an enemy, if it extends to others, it is termed "diffuse" (*màn*); thus, what was "overcoming" (*kè*) becomes "diffuse.

As for the previous statement—that when the intent to overcome is equivalent to the actual act, it constitutes a grave offense—this should be explained with reference to material wealth, which can be distinguished accordingly.
As illustrated by the following example: there is one primary offender, namely hatred (*dveṣa*). Hatred is the fundamental thief; the others are secondary thieves.

When those secondary thieves cause death through mutual dependence, the one who harbored hatred commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), because the mental state and the objective circumstance correspond. As for the others, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense, as the conditions for killing were not fully met.
Because there was no intentional mind to kill them, as in the following distinct case:
according to the Vinaya, when preaching the Dharma to nuns, one must not continue until sunset;

however, if one preaches the Dharma to laypeople at a ferry crossing where nuns happen to be listening, it does not constitute an offense, because the nuns are not the primary intended recipients of the teaching. This principle applies to other cases such as lying and so forth.
"Listen. In principle, this should not constitute an offense.

Now, [the text] below first refutes [this view]. Regarding 'avoiding suspicion': according to the Vinaya, because Nanda preached the Dharma until dusk, the bhikṣuṇīs stayed overnight in the moat of Jetavana and incurred public censure.
Subsequently, although preaching was permitted, it was not allowed to continue until dusk. All of these [restrictions] were intended to prevent the suspicions and slanders of the laity."

That is so. This [offense of] lying belongs to the category of prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*), whereas this *pārājika* offense belongs to the category of intrinsic gravity (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

One cannot use the latter to serve as an analogy for the former. To explain further: regarding the objects of the offense, one commits a *pārājika* with a human; a *sthūlātyaya* with a non-human; and a *sthūlātyaya* with an intelligent animal.
"Absence of wisdom is auspicious.

Both [terms] are read with a downward tone. Generally speaking, regarding "errors," there are two types: general and specific. In the general sense, any discrepancy between mind and object is termed an error.
The distinctions are explained according to the specific matters; there are different paths for these characteristics. The first "so" (then/therefore) explains the reasons for the distinctions;
the second "so" interrogates and explains the different paths, as can be understood from the text itself.
There is no "light" offense. By means of this single precept, one does not take into account the confusion of objects or the delusion of the mind.

Why is this? The affliction of desire is the intensity of its poison; the failure of desire is the depth of its obstruction. Therefore, it is specifically prescribed that neither error nor delusion shall be taken into consideration.

However, there is a "light" [offense] if one applies the right path with the thought that it is a wrong path; or, to explain the "light" [offense] regarding delusion, it refers to the preceding state of mind.
This refers to the following: the latter mind is what is meant by "that. The phrase "object below" (*jing xia*) is an error in the commentary;
